topics.name: The most famous quotes
topics.title: The Most Famous Moby-Dick Quotes, Ranked
topics.description: The most famous quotes from Moby-Dick, from “Call me Ishmael” down, each shown in its verse with chapter and verse and checked against the text.
intro: Plenty of people who have never read Moby-Dick can quote its first three words. These are the lines that got out of the book: the ones that turn up in sermons, on tote bags, in tattoos and in other people’s novels.

They run roughly from most famous to least. That order is a judgment call, so feel free to argue with it. The famous line is picked out inside each verse, and every one is checked against the text of the novel.
topics.card_line: Call me Ishmael.

topics.name: Ahab
topics.title: Captain Ahab Quotes from Moby-Dick
topics.description: Captain Ahab in Moby-Dick: the passages where he speaks, broods and commands, from the quarter-deck to the final chase, with chapter and verse.
intro: Captain of the Pequod, owner of one ivory leg and one idea. Ahab does not come on deck until Chapter 28, and by then the book has spent a long time warning you about him. Captain Peleg calls him “a grand, ungodly, god-like man”.

These are the passages where he speaks, broods, commands and burns: from the quarter-deck, where he nails a gold doubloon to the mast, to the last day of the chase. Read them in order and you can watch a man become his own weather.
topics.card_line: Talk not to me of blasphemy, man; I’d strike the sun if it insulted me.

topics.name: The White Whale
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About the White Whale
topics.description: Every passage about Moby Dick, the white whale, from sailors' rumours and Ahab's scars to the three-day chase that ends the novel.
intro: He gives the book its name, yet he only appears in the flesh in its last three chapters. Everything before that is rumour, sighting, scar and theory: tales swapped with passing ships, Ahab’s missing leg, and a whole chapter on the horror of his colour.
These passages follow Moby Dick through the novel, first as a legend and then as something that breaches. This site never draws him, but here, at least, he can be named.
topics.card_line: It was the whiteness of the whale that above all things appalled me.

topics.name: Ishmael
topics.title: Ishmael Quotes from Moby-Dick
topics.description: Ishmael, the narrator of Moby-Dick: the passages where he steps out from behind the whales and the crew to speak for himself, with chapter and verse.
intro: “Call me Ishmael.” The narrator gives you three words of introduction and then very little else: an empty purse, a damp, drizzly November in his soul, and the habit of going to sea whenever he feels grim about the mouth.

For long stretches he all but disappears behind the whales, the crew and Ahab. These are some of the passages where he steps back into view: a schoolmaster turned whaleman, Queequeg’s bosom friend, and in the end the only one left to tell the story.
topics.card_line: I am tormented with an everlasting itch for things remote.

topics.name: Queequeg
topics.title: Queequeg Quotes from Moby-Dick
topics.description: Queequeg in Moby-Dick: harpooneer, prince of Kokovoko and Ishmael's bosom friend. Every passage he appears in, with chapter and verse.
intro: Harpooneer, prince of the island of Kokovoko, seller of embalmed heads, and the best friend anyone in the novel has. Ishmael’s first night with him, sharing a bed at the Spouter-Inn, is a comedy of terror. By the morning he has decided: “Better sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian.”

Here he is wherever the tags could find him: at the harpoon, at prayer before his little idol Yojo, diving overboard to save a man who mocked him, and lying in the coffin he asked the ship’s carpenter to make.
topics.card_line: Better sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian.

topics.name: Starbuck
topics.title: Starbuck Quotes from Moby-Dick
topics.description: Starbuck, the Pequod's chief mate: the voice of caution in Moby-Dick and the one man who tells Ahab to his face that the hunt is madness.
intro: The chief mate, a Nantucketer of Quaker stock: brave, but never reckless, and the one man aboard who tells Ahab to his face that this is madness. His rule for whaleboats is simple. “I will have no man in my boat,” said Starbuck, “who is not afraid of a whale.”
These passages follow the voice of caution through a voyage that will not listen to it, including the night he stands outside Ahab’s cabin with a loaded musket in his hands.
topics.card_line: Vengeance on a dumb brute!

topics.name: Obsession
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Obsession
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about obsession and monomania: how one purpose takes hold of Ahab, his crew and the whole voyage. With chapter and verse.
intro: Melville’s word for it is monomania: one idea that eats all the others. Ahab’s idea is a single whale, and he explains it to Starbuck in a sentence that never quite lets go: “He tasks me; he heaps me.”
These are the passages where one purpose takes over a man, then a ship, then thirty-odd souls who signed up to hunt whales for oil. Read them alongside Madness and Revenge, which are never far away.
topics.card_line: The path to my fixed purpose is laid with iron rails, whereon my soul is grooved to run.

topics.name: Revenge
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Revenge
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about revenge and vengeance: Ahab's oath on the quarter-deck, Starbuck's objection, and the chase that follows.
intro: The whale took Ahab’s leg, and Ahab wants the whale. On the quarter-deck in Chapter 36 he turns a voyage for oil into a vendetta, and only Starbuck objects: “Vengeance on a dumb brute!”
Here are the passages where vengeance is sworn, toasted, questioned and pursued to the end, all the way to Ahab’s last words to the whale.
topics.card_line: from hell’s heart I stab at thee; for hate’s sake I spit my last breath at thee.

topics.name: Fate
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Fate
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about fate, prophecy and destiny: Elijah's warning, Fedallah's hearses and a voyage that seems already written.
intro: Moby-Dick is full of prophets: Elijah on the Nantucket wharf, Gabriel raving aboard the Jeroboam, Fedallah with his riddle of two hearses. Even Ishmael, weaving a mat in Chapter 47, decides that chance, free will and necessity are all at work together.
These are the passages where the voyage seems already written and the characters half know it. It is hard to read them without feeling the ending coming.
topics.card_line: we are turned round and round in this world, like yonder windlass, and Fate is the handspike.

topics.name: Death
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Death
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about death and mortality, from the whaleman's chapel and its memorial tablets to the coffin that ends the book.
intro: The book opens with a man who catches himself “pausing before coffin warehouses” and ends with a coffin used as a life-buoy. In between come memorial tablets, a will, sharks and a great many whales.

Ishmael’s own view is surprisingly cheerful: “Methinks we have hugely mistaken this matter of Life and Death.” These are the passages where death comes close, from the whaleman’s chapel in New Bedford to the last page.
topics.card_line: Methinks we have hugely mistaken this matter of Life and Death.

topics.name: Isolation and Loneliness
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Isolation and Loneliness
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about isolation and loneliness: the crew of Isolatoes, Ahab alone with his charts and Pip lost in the open sea.
intro: Ishmael calls the crew Isolatoes, men “not acknowledging the common continent of men”, each living on an island of his own. Then there is Ahab, alone below decks with his charts, and Pip, left alone in the open sea until his mind leaves him.
These are the novel’s loneliest passages, and there are a lot of them.
topics.card_line: in the soul of man there lies one insular Tahiti, full of peace and joy

topics.name: The Sea
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About the Sea
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about the sea and the ocean: its calms, its storms, its meadows of brit and the pull it has on everyone ashore.
intro: Ishmael goes to sea whenever he feels grim about the mouth, and he insists that everyone feels the same pull. On a Sunday afternoon in Manhattan, he says, thousands of city-dwellers stand at the water’s edge, “fixed in ocean reveries.”
Across the novel the sea is a mirror, a grave, a pasture and something close to a god. These passages gather its moods, from the calm of the Pacific to the typhoon.
topics.card_line: meditation and water are wedded for ever.

topics.name: Man vs. Nature
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Man vs. Nature
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about man against nature: small boats, vast whales, typhoons and an ocean that does not care either way.
intro: Whaling, as Melville tells it, is a small wooden boat against the largest animal on earth, on an ocean that does not care either way. “Consider the subtleness of the sea,” he writes; “how its most dreaded creatures glide under water, unapparent for the most part.”
These passages are about that contest: storms and calms, fire on the masts, and the whale itself, which has the last word.
topics.card_line: the great shroud of the sea rolled on as it rolled five thousand years ago.

topics.name: Madness
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Madness
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about madness and insanity: Ahab's sane means and mad purpose, Pip's vision in the sea and a ship of mad prophets.
intro: Ahab knows exactly what he is: “all my means are sane, my motive and my object mad.” Starbuck calls the hunt madness, Pip loses his mind in the open sea, and the Jeroboam sails under the spell of a mad prophet.
Melville does not treat madness simply as an illness. Of Pip he writes: “So man’s insanity is heaven’s sense.” These passages gather the madness of the voyage, and the wisdom hidden in some of it.
topics.card_line: There is a wisdom that is woe; but there is a woe that is madness.

topics.name: God and Faith
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About God and Faith
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about God, faith and religion: Father Mapple's sermon, Queequeg's idol Yojo and Ahab defying the fire.
intro: Before he ever sees a whale, Ishmael sits through Father Mapple’s sermon on Jonah, preached from a pulpit you climb by rope ladder. Soon afterwards he joins Queequeg in worshipping a small wooden idol, and talks himself into it as a good Presbyterian.
The novel argues with God all the way through, from the sermon and Queequeg’s Ramadan to Ahab defying the fire in “The Candles”. These passages gather its faith, its doubt and its blasphemy.
topics.card_line: Is it I, God, or who, that lifts this arm?

topics.name: Friendship
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Friendship
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about friendship and companionship: Ishmael and Queequeg, the monkey-rope and the brotherhood of the crew.
intro: The warmest thing in Moby-Dick is the friendship between Ishmael and Queequeg. It starts with terror in a shared bed and turns, within a day, into something that mends Ishmael’s spirits: “I felt a melting in me.”
These are the passages about companionship at sea: shipmates and bosom friends, the monkey-rope that ties two men’s lives together, and a tub of spermaceti squeezed in brotherly love.
topics.card_line: see how elastic our stiff prejudices grow when love once comes to bend them.

topics.name: Whales
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Whales
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about whales: the sperm whale, the right whale, the leviathan of scripture and Ishmael's cetology, with chapter and verse.
intro: Moby-Dick is also a book about whales in general, sometimes to its readers’ despair. Ishmael sorts them like a librarian in “Cetology”, measures their skeletons, reviews their portraits and puzzles over their spouts.
His definition is splendidly simple: a whale is “a spouting fish with a horizontal tail.” These passages gather the sperm whale, the right whale, the leviathan of scripture and the rest of the pod.
topics.card_line: Oh, man! admire and model thyself after the whale!

topics.name: Stubb
topics.title: Stubb Quotes from Moby-Dick
topics.description: Stubb, the Pequod's second mate: the pipe, the jokes and the whale-steak supper, in every passage where he speaks or acts, with chapter and verse.
intro: The second mate, from Cape Cod, and never without his pipe. Stubb treats a whale hunt like a job and a typhoon like weather. His philosophy fits on a card: “Think not, is my eleventh commandment; and sleep when you can, is my twelfth.”

He is the book’s best company and not always its best man. He mocks the cook, abandons Pip to the sea and eats whale by whale-light. These are his passages, from the first lowering to his last joke: “I know not all that may be coming, but be it what it will, I’ll go to it laughing.”
topics.card_line: Think not, is my eleventh commandment; and sleep when you can, is my twelfth

topics.name: Flask
topics.title: Flask Quotes from Moby-Dick
topics.description: Flask, the Pequod's third mate from Martha's Vineyard: the passages where the smallest officer on board does his work, with chapter and verse.
intro: The third mate is “a short, stout, ruddy young fellow” from Martha’s Vineyard, so fond of a fight with a whale that he takes it as a personal insult. The crew call him King-Post, after a short, square timber in a ship’s frame.

Flask has little time for awe or omens. A whale, to him, is a sort of magnified mouse. To see over the waves he climbs onto the shoulders of Daggoo, the tallest harpooneer, and stands there quite at home. These are his passages.
topics.card_line: with one dexterous fling landed the little man high and dry on his shoulders.

topics.name: Pip
topics.title: Pip Quotes from Moby-Dick
topics.description: Pip, the Pequod's youngest sailor: the passages about the boy left alone in the sea, his madness and his bond with Ahab, with chapter and verse.
intro: The smallest and youngest on board, a boy who plays the tambourine. Pip is drafted into a whaleboat, jumps out in fright and is left behind in the open sea. When he is picked up, something in him has gone. “The sea had jeeringly kept his finite body up, but drowned the infinite of his soul.”

Afterwards he speaks in riddles, and the riddles are often the truest lines in the book. Ahab, who listens to no one, takes him into his cabin. These are Pip’s passages, from the tambourine to “Pip! Pip! Pip!”
topics.card_line: The sea had jeeringly kept his finite body up, but drowned the infinite of his soul.

topics.name: The harpooneers
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About the Harpooneers
topics.description: Tashtego, Daggoo and the Pequod's other harpooneers: the passages about the men who throw the irons, with chapter and verse.
intro: Every whaleboat carries a harpooneer in the bow. On the Pequod that means Queequeg, who has a page of his own, Tashtego, from Gay Head on Martha’s Vineyard, and Daggoo. “Third among the harpooneers was Daggoo,” a giant with a lion-like tread.

These are the men who stand up first when the whale is close. Tashtego falls headfirst into a sinking whale’s head and has to be cut out of it. In the final chapter, he is still nailing the flag to the mast as the ship goes down.
topics.card_line: It’s a mutual, joint-stock world, in all meridians. We cannibals must help these Christians.

topics.name: Fedallah
topics.title: Fedallah Quotes from Moby-Dick
topics.description: Fedallah, Ahab's secret harpooneer: the passages about the silent Parsee and his prophecies, with chapter and verse.
intro: At the first lowering, Ahab’s own boat crew climbs out of hiding. Nobody on the Pequod knew they were aboard. At their head is Fedallah, the Parsee: tall, silent, turbaned, and to the crew something closer to a shadow than a shipmate.

He speaks rarely, and when he does it is prophecy. Before Ahab can die, Fedallah says, he will see two hearses on the sea; and “Hemp only can kill thee.” These are the passages where he appears, or watches.
topics.card_line: Hemp only can kill thee.

topics.name: Peleg and Bildad
topics.title: Peleg and Bildad Quotes from Moby-Dick
topics.description: Captains Peleg and Bildad, the Quaker owners of the Pequod: the passages where they sign on Ishmael and send the ship to sea, with chapter and verse.
intro: Two retired whaling captains, both Quakers and both part-owners of the Pequod. Peleg swears like a sailor; Bildad reads scripture and drives a hard bargain. While haggling over Ishmael’s pay, he murmurs, “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth.”

They hire the crew, stock the hold and warn Ishmael about the captain he has not yet met. Then they pilot the ship out of harbour and go home. These are their passages, almost all in the chapters before the voyage begins.
topics.card_line: _Lay_ not up for yourselves treasures upon earth

topics.name: Father Mapple and Jonah
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Jonah and Father Mapple
topics.description: Father Mapple's sermon on Jonah and every other mention of Jonah in Moby-Dick: the passages, with chapter and verse.
intro: Before the voyage, Ishmael goes to the Whaleman’s Chapel in New Bedford. Father Mapple, an old harpooneer turned preacher, climbs into a pulpit shaped like a ship’s bow by a rope ladder, pulls the ladder up behind him and preaches on Jonah. “And God had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah.”

Jonah keeps surfacing after that, in jokes, in arguments about whether a whale could swallow a man, and in the book’s long worry about running from God. These are his passages, and the sermon that ends “Delight is to him”.
topics.card_line: And God had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah.

topics.name: The Pequod
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About the Pequod
topics.description: The Pequod, Ahab's whaling ship: the passages describing her, her crew and her voyage, from Nantucket harbour to the last chapter.
intro: Ishmael picks her himself, from three ships in Nantucket harbour. She is old, weather-stained and decorated all over with whale bone and teeth, “a cannibal of a craft, tricking herself forth in the chased bones of her enemies.”

Her name comes from a tribe of Native Americans, and Ishmael calls her a noble craft, “but somehow a most melancholy! All noble things are touched with that.” These are the passages about the ship herself, from her deck and her tiller to the place where she goes down.
topics.card_line: A cannibal of a craft, tricking herself forth in the chased bones of her enemies.

topics.name: Fear
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Fear
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about fear, dread and terror: of the sea, of the whale and of the unknown, with chapter and verse.
intro: Whaling is a frightening trade, and the book is honest about it: the lowering, the line whipping past your ear, the whale that turns on the boat. But the fear Ishmael lingers over is stranger. “It was the whiteness of the whale that above all things appalled me.”

These passages run from ordinary terror to the nameless kind: dread of a captain, of the dark, of what might be under the water. Courage in this book is not the absence of fear but the habit of going on with it.
topics.card_line: Ignorance is the parent of fear

topics.name: Identity
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Identity
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about identity and the self: who we are at sea, in the dark and among strangers, with chapter and verse.
intro: A narrator who will not say his real name, a harpooneer far from his island, a captain who becomes his own obsession. Moby-Dick keeps asking who people are once their homes are behind them.

Ishmael’s answer is partly that we only know ourselves with the lights out: “no man can ever feel his own identity aright except his eyes be closed.” These passages gather the book’s thinking on the self, from the first night in the Spouter-Inn onwards.
topics.card_line: no man can ever feel his own identity aright except his eyes be closed

topics.name: Leadership and authority
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Leadership and Authority
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about leadership, command and authority aboard a whaling ship, with chapter and verse.
intro: A whaling ship is a small kingdom, and its captain answers to no one once land is out of sight. Ahab knows it. When Starbuck stands up to him, he puts it plainly: “There is one God that is Lord over the earth, and one Captain that is lord over the Pequod.”

These passages are about who gives orders and why anyone obeys: mates and harpooneers, owners and crew, and a captain who turns a commercial voyage into a private war. Watch how often the book asks whether anyone could have stopped him.
topics.card_line: There is one God that is Lord over the earth, and one Captain that is lord over the Pequod.

topics.name: Rebellion and mutiny
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Rebellion and Mutiny
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about rebellion and mutiny, from the Town-Ho's story to Starbuck's doubts, with chapter and verse.
intro: Mutiny hangs over the Pequod without ever quite breaking out. Its fullest version happens on another ship. In “The Town-Ho’s Story”, told over drinks in Lima, a sailor called Steelkilt is pushed too far by a bullying mate.

Closer to home, Starbuck stands at Ahab’s door one night with a loaded musket and asks himself whether to use it. These passages are about the limits of obedience at sea: when a crew follows, when it balks, and what it costs either way.
topics.card_line: I’ll hold the musket boldly while I think.

topics.name: Pride
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Pride
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about pride and hubris, above all Ahab's, with chapter and verse.
intro: Ahab smashes his quadrant because it cannot tell him where the whale is. When lightning reverses his compasses, he makes new needles himself and shows them to the crew. “In his fiery eyes of scorn and triumph, you then saw Ahab in all his fatal pride.”
Pride in Moby-Dick is mostly a captain’s, but not only his. These passages gather the moments when someone refuses to bend, to the sea, to sense or to God, and what the book thinks of them for it.
topics.card_line: In his fiery eyes of scorn and triumph, you then saw Ahab in all his fatal pride.

topics.name: Perception and reality
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Perception and Reality
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about perception, illusion and reality: how the same whale, coin or sea looks different to each viewer, with chapter and verse.
intro: Ahab nails a gold doubloon to the mast, and one by one the crew stop to read it. Each sees himself. Pip, watching them, sums it up in a conjugation: “I look, you look, he looks; we look, ye look, they look.”

The whole book works this way. A whale is a fish, a god, a profit or a devil depending on who is looking, and the sea is never only what it appears. These passages are about the gap between what is seen and what is there.
topics.card_line: All visible objects, man, are but as pasteboard masks.

topics.name: Despair
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Despair
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about despair, desperation and grief, with chapter and verse.
intro: For a book that starts with a joke about knocking people’s hats off, Moby-Dick goes to some dark places. Ishmael goes to sea to escape a gloom he cannot shake, and he meets plenty of it on the way.

Watching the try-works burn at night, he warns against staring too long into the fire, and draws a line: “There is a wisdom that is woe; but there is a woe that is madness.” These passages sit on both sides of it, from desperate moments in the boats to Ahab’s private grief.
topics.card_line: God! God! God!—crack my heart!—stave my brain!

topics.name: Courage and defiance
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Courage and Defiance
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about courage, bravery and defiance, at sea and on deck, with chapter and verse.
intro: Everyone on a whaleboat needs courage, but the book is wary of the wrong kind. Starbuck will not have a man in his boat who is not afraid of a whale, because “an utterly fearless man is a far more dangerous comrade than a coward.”

Defiance is Ahab’s mode, aimed at the whale, the weather and the gods. These passages set the two side by side: the steady courage of the men in the boats and the louder defiance of the man on the quarter-deck.
topics.card_line: an utterly fearless man is a far more dangerous comrade than a coward.

topics.name: Mystery and the unknown
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Mystery and the Unknown
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about mystery and the unknown: the sea, the whale and whatever lies beneath, with chapter and verse.
intro: Ishmael goes to sea for the same reason Narcissus looked into the water: to chase an image that cannot be caught. He calls it “the ungraspable phantom of life”.

From then on, the unknown is everywhere: in the depths under the boats, behind the whale’s blank forehead, in the silent Parsee and in Ahab’s plans. These passages are about what the book cannot, or will not, explain.
topics.card_line: It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all.

topics.name: Awe and the sublime
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Awe and the Sublime
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about awe, wonder and the sublime: whales, oceans and storms too big to take in, with chapter and verse.
intro: Much of Moby-Dick is a man trying to describe something too big to describe. Whales a hundred feet long, a Pacific that rolls “a thousand leagues of blue”, a sea that seems to breathe.

In the Grand Armada, Ishmael’s boat drifts into the calm centre of a vast school of whales, where mothers nurse their young. In that stillness he finds a calm in himself too. These passages are where the book stops to stare.
topics.card_line: amid the tornadoed Atlantic of my being, do I myself still for ever centrally disport in mute calm

topics.name: Humour
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Humour
topics.description: The funny side of Moby-Dick: jokes, comic scenes and the book's dry wit, with chapter and verse.
intro: People expect Moby-Dick to be heavy. It is also very funny: two strangers forced to share a bed, a sermon to sharks, an argument about whether a whale is a fish.

Ishmael even has a theory of it. At certain moments a man “takes this whole universe for a vast practical joke” and decides the joke is mostly on him. These are the passages where the book is laughing, sometimes in the face of death.
topics.card_line: I know not all that may be coming, but be it what it will, I’ll go to it laughing.

topics.name: Melancholy
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Melancholy
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about melancholy, gloom and sorrow, with chapter and verse.
intro: The novel begins with “a damp, drizzly November in my soul” and treats the sea as a cure for it. It works, more or less, but the mood never quite lifts.

Ishmael finds sadness even in the ship that will carry him: a noble craft, “but somehow a most melancholy! All noble things are touched with that.” These passages are the book’s quieter, greyer moments, from the opening page to the long watches at sea.
topics.card_line: whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul

topics.name: The hunt
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About the Hunt
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about hunting whales: the lookouts, the lowerings, the chases and the kills, with chapter and verse.
intro: “There she blows!” For long stretches the Pequod is a ship full of men waiting for those words. When they come, the boats drop, the oars bend and the chase begins.

These passages follow the work of whaling: the mast-head watch, the race to the whale, the harpoon and the line, and the long fight that follows. They end with the hunt the whole voyage was for, three days long, against one whale.
topics.card_line: There she blows!

topics.name: Storms and weather
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Storms and Weather
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about storms, typhoons, lightning and calm: the weather on the Pequod's voyage, with chapter and verse.
intro: In the Japan grounds the Pequod runs into a typhoon. Lightning strikes, the masts burn with pale fire at their tips, and Ahab holds the lightning chain and speaks to the flames. To him it is a sign: “the white flame but lights the way to the White Whale.”
These passages track the book’s weather, from squalls and gales to the glassy calms where nothing moves. At sea the sky is never just scenery; it is the boss.
topics.card_line: the white flame but lights the way to the White Whale

topics.name: Nantucket
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Nantucket
topics.description: Nantucket in Moby-Dick: the island, its whalemen and the harbour where the Pequod sets sail, with chapter and verse.
intro: “Nantucket! Take out your map and look at it.” A mere hillock of sand far out at sea, Ishmael says, so bare that a piece of wood is treated like a holy relic. No wonder its people took to the water instead.

It is where the Pequod sails from, and home to Ahab, Starbuck and the ship’s owners. These passages cover the island and its people, from the try-pots of the inn to the whalemen who own the sea “as Emperors own empires.”
topics.card_line: Nantucket! Take out your map and look at it.

topics.name: The doubloon
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About the Doubloon
topics.description: The gold doubloon Ahab nails to the Pequod's mast as a reward, and what each man sees in it, with chapter and verse.
intro: On the quarter-deck, Ahab nails a gold coin from Ecuador to the mainmast and promises it to the first man who sights the white whale. From then on it hangs there, catching the light, a prize and a mirror at once.
Later Ahab, Starbuck, Stubb, Flask and others stop in turn to read its signs, and each finds something different. Pip has the last word: “I look, you look, he looks; we look, ye look, they look.”
topics.card_line: I look, you look, he looks; we look, ye look, they look.

topics.name: Survival
topics.title: Moby-Dick Quotes About Survival
topics.description: Passages from Moby-Dick about survival at sea: close calls, rescues and the one man left to tell the story, with chapter and verse.
intro: Whaling ships came home short of men as a matter of course. On the Pequod, staying alive means trusting a monkey-rope, a shipmate and a lot of luck.

Only one man survives the voyage, and only because a coffin built for someone else bobs up beside him. “Buoyed up by that coffin, for almost one whole day and night, I floated on a soft and dirgelike main.” These passages are about getting through, from the first lowering to the epilogue.
topics.card_line: Buoyed up by that coffin, for almost one whole day and night, I floated on a soft and dirgelike main.
